title: AITSL's Review of the Teaching Standards: The Good, the Bad and the Vaguely Defined
author: Caiti Wade
summary: Caiti Wade gives a live, opinionated summary of the 61-page discussion paper from the Australian Institute for Teaching and School Leadership (AITSL) reviewing the Australian Professional Standards for Teachers, with submissions open until 20 November. She explains what the standards are, why teachers must evidence them to progress through the Graduate, Proficient, Highly Accomplished and Lead stages, and how the review used a literature review, expert submissions and an open survey. Her own standing criticism is that the standards are too broad to act on and are not clearly linked to the evidence on how students learn, noting that the standard on knowing how students learn never cites that research. She then works through the seven improvement areas the review identifies, adding her reactions and caveats throughout. Her closing view is that a national framework should reflect what is known about effective practice and help teachers reflect, find professional learning and improve, and that the review leaves her a little more hopeful.
points: The review names seven improvement areas, and Wade welcomes its direction while stressing that the paper is a discussion document and not a set of final recommendations.
Standard 1, know students and how they learn, does not reference research on how students learn in any focus area, which she regards as a significant gap.
Broad descriptors such as differentiation can send teachers toward planning several lessons in one instead of providing supports for the core content.
Because evidence of practice is weighted more heavily than the practice itself, the standards risk becoming a compliance exercise that rewording alone cannot fix.
A national framework need not be a pedagogical playbook, but it should help teachers reflect on practice, identify growth areas and become better teachers.
quotes: The purpose of the review is essentially to consider where the standards could be improved, including considering relevance and whether they align with the evidence on effective teaching practice.

To summarise some of my main thoughts, on the surface, the standards seem fine; however, they’re far to broad to be actionable and are not clearly and explicitly linked to the evidence base around how students learn, for instance.

Another core point I’ve made previously about the current standards is that standard 1 is “know students and how they learn”, but doesn’t once reference the research around how students learn in any focus area.
it is underpinned by my usual bias and opinions. This isn’t intended to be an objective review.

This is also a bigger issue with the systems and processes that turn the standards into compliance exercises where providing evidence of practice is weighted more heavily than applying the practice itself.

While I don’t expect the Australian Professional Standards for Teachers to act as a comprehensive pedagogical playbook (and honestly, I don’t think they should), I do think it’s reasonable to expect that a national framework describing what teachers should know and be able to do reflects our understanding of effective practice.

In essence, if we’re going to have professional standards for teachers, surely those standards should help us to reflect on our practice, identify professional learning and growth opportunities, and then become better teachers.
